title: When making games, do you think story first or mechanics first?
author: katatonicmango
selftext:
Here is the video explaining my process for my latest game Royal Flush: [https://youtu.be/EIk4wMBHQ70?si=yi490pzemQZw94Zo](https://youtu.be/EIk4wMBHQ70?si=yi490pzemQZw94Zo)

You can play Royal Flush here: [https://kedikatstudios.itch.io/royal-flush](https://kedikatstudios.itch.io/royal-flush)



My partner and I have very different methods for creating games with Claude code. I personally like to have a story worked out first, then think of game mechanics that support it. My partner gets inspired by gameplay for example, I want to make a tank battle game/ first person shooter, then he adds on a story to fit the gameplay. 

  
How do you guys go about things? I like to think my method saves credits ha, but I'm not sure. 



For this game I used Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code. 



* Before any code, Claude and I wrote a checklist: the pitch, the controls, three 90-second levels, and a style guide (low-poly PS1 look, 1996-era).
* Early on I asked for a robot play tester that plays every level after each change, including runs where it makes mistakes on purpose.
* Most of the day was 13 rounds of feedback on the look and feel.

  
I guess I like having a roadmap before starting anything. Not entirely a game design document, but like a one pager that explains the gist of the game. How do you guys do it?

comments.author: dalonelygamer88
comments.body:
It will depend on the game you are making. 

If you want a story driven game then obviously the goal should be to make the beginning middle and end first then fleshout the details. 

If you are making a mechanics driven game (like I am) then the selling point should be the mechanics of the game and you should have that first. 

  
For a story game who cares if you can loot every container and craft 50mil items we are here for the story. 

For a mechanics driven game who cares you are living in a dystopian world and your handler Greg died. Im here to do this dystopian job for the company.

comments.author: Physical-Bite-3837
comments.body: Narrative-heavy genres like RPGs and story-driven adventure games probably require an established plot outline prior to creation. Otherwise mechanics-driven titles like platformers only require a basic premise to get started and you can throw in a story later.

replies.author: katatonicmango
replies.body: Which do you prefer making/ playing?

replies.author: Physical-Bite-3837
replies.body: Mostly the latter, although I do love a really good story in an rpg.

comments.author: tkbillington
comments.body: If the mechanics aren’t fun nobody will progress in your story so I start on mechanics according to my logic. And it’s killed 5/6 of my games so far lol

comments.author: throwaway275275275
comments.body: Mechanics first, otherwise it's a story and not a game, why not write a book ? That's a much better medium to deliver a story. A game has to be a game first

comments.author: Ok-Pirate5732
comments.body:
I went Setting>Game Genre>Mechanics 

What historical era is really interesting but underrepresented? What type of game would fit well into this setting? What type of mechanics would be unique (and fun of course) to the history we're retelling?
